summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. 1966 and March 31st, 1967 in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the money lent investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Wealth Tax officer sought support from a judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Veda Prakash Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth tax [AIR 1970 SC 311. The Appellate Assistant Com missioner held that the judgment of this Court was binding and accordingly by a consolidated order dated April 3, 1972. The Commissioner then appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, 309 ^ HELD: Under section 2(q) the net wealth of an assessee has to be determined as it obtains on a particular date. That is the "valuation date". Clause (q) of s 2 defines the expression " valuation date", as follows: "the amount by which the aggregate value. Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate Value of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation day." [310 A] In the instant case the assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valued date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset.

The appellants and the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff instituted a suit No. 157 of 1968 for a declaration and injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do in Predio ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was not in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit for declaration simpliciter could not lie. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the suit was barred by res judicata as held by this Court in Dhondi Tukaram vs Hari Dadu AIR 1954 Bom 100; that the claim based on the factum of tenancy was not based on such allegation; and that the lease had terminated by efflux of time and defendant No 2 was, therefore entitled to let out the property to one of the defendants. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The decision rendered by the Civil Court would be without jurisdiction and, accordingly, it is directed that the issue whether defendant No1 was a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil court stood ousted by Section 58(2) of the Act. [1024B] 2. A mere declaration of his status as a tenant could not be granted unless the consequential relief for possession was prayed. The suit was filed on the basis that defendant No 1 was a trespasser and the plaintiff who had been dispossessed, by an act of trespass, lost his rights in the property. [ 1026C D] 3. So long as the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit, the relief for land could not he gone into by the civil Court in view of the clear language of Section 7 read with Section 58 (2) specifically bars the jurisdiction to all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to he settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1009G] 4. The jurisdiction of Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2), of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any dispute which is by or under the Act required to been settled, decide and dealt with in accordance with the Mamlatdar 's recommendation. There can, therefore be no doubt that after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Tenancy Act, and had, therefore in order to get back his possession he was entitled to recover immediate possession of it on the strength of his tenancy.

The petitioners are engaged as carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the ' Corpo ration). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". Their claim is resisted by the respondents contending that the petitioners are doing the same duties and performing similar functions as that of "Senior Speech Therapist", "Audiologist" and "Speech Pathologist". Allowing the petition and dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: (1) It is not just a comparison of physical activity. [669C] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (2) In service merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or she learns also by experience as much as by other means. [668B C] (3) The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical location though owned by a same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the life in the same establishment, the principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" cannot be enforced. [ 667B C D] (4) In the instant case the petitioners were employed by a Company incorporated under the and they can not claim wages payable to their counterparts situated in Government service. They cannot enforce the right to equal pay for Equal pay for equally work. The discrimination alleged against must be beyond the same liabi fide value owned by them. A distinction cannot be ex tended with counter affidavit in other establishment with different Management, or Even in establishments where there is no such distinction amongst the identical set Of employees by any one master in the Same establishment, that the principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The discriminatory discrimination complained was only within the domain of Articles 14 and 16 which provides for equal pay in a particular cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [667F G] (5) It would be irrational to suggest that equal pay should be payable for equal appoint ment to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. A reference cannot be mad ed to the decision in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognition) vs Unionof India, AIR 1962 SC 1688, followed.

P.C. and the confirmation of conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1, S, S and S.S. was set aside. The High Court allowed the appeal filed by accused 2 and 6 and acquitted him of that charge. Dismissing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1(i) The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 4 in this case in view of section 32 of the Indian Penal Code and no appeal was filed in this Court against the acquittal by accused B.

The appellant daughter was married to one S on August 22, 1945, and according to the will the respondent I was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 thereof. After the death of his father Sadagopalachar she became the absolute owner of all the properties including the suit property which had been inherited by her from her husband. It was also contended that after S having taken a leading part in its execution, she was in a sound disposing state of mind, that it represented her intentions and that it was for this reason she had relinquished her interest in the properties and waived her right to dispose them by a will and that after the death the document would remain with the appellant. Held, that the onus of proving the execution of the will lies in every case upon the party propounding a will. It is not proper to argue that mere entries in the revenue record made in the name of Sadag Mawlavachar or the long possession of Sadahalachar and after his death no other issue survived for decision. Parker vs Felgate, (18) L.R. 70 I.A. 53, relied on. It would be a part of the initial onus to remove any legitimate doubts in the matter of execution of a will which is put before the testator as carrying it out and that if there are suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution or of the Will the propounder must remove the said suspicions from the mind of the court by cogent and satisfactory evidence.

The appellants, their firm manufacturing Arcons (Cinema Arcbons) manufactured by the appellants were being assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77. Sometime thereafter they had also filed returns in respect of them under consideration. The question was whether the goods falling within entry 41 of Schedule 1, that entry required the taxable object with its general or ordinary use. The High Court referred to the fact that the appellants had not produced their account books to show that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. Dismissing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1. A perusal of the entry under consideration links the taxable justification with its vide general or popular use would be the language actually employed by them. [562H] 2. The word 'accessories ' is used in several entries such as entry No. 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, Entry No. 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speakers. [564B C] 3. The terms 'accessory ' in section 2 of the Act cannot be restricted to particular machines for which they are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. [565E G] 4. The expression "accessories" is used with a view to defining the goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition and therefore, it could not be said that any useful purpose was served by multiplying cases relating to entries which are so very different and could have only a very remote hearing, if any, upon any reasoning which could be adopted to support the submission that the arc carbons under consideration were covered by the relevant entry No.[565C] 5. The appellants ' plea of appeal before the High Court was not accepted. [567F G] 6. The order of the High court setting aside the order of assessment is quashed and set aside.

Rule 21 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966 provides that a holder of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under these rules shall pay royalty in respect of minor minerals provided in column 2 of the schedule removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the rates specified against them in column 3 of the Schedule. It further provides that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of village potters if their annual produc tion is not exceeding two lakh bricks and they supply at least one lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. The petitioners were lessees of a parwana granted under the Rules. They challenged the validity of Rule 21 as it existed prior to the issue of the impugned Notification by filing writ petitions in this Court which had been dismissed. In the meantime, the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules 1966 came into force and the Rules were framed with regard to the grant of prospecting licences and mining leases. The validity of these rules was considered in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and Ors., ; and as required by Rule 21 a Full Bench of this Court held that under Entry 50 of List II of 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the State Government had to be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose sanctioned by law. In view of the above decision, the petitioners were called upon to pay a sum of Rs.2,000 by way of costs to the State of Maharashtra. The Writ Petitions filed in this court challenging the validity and validity of Rules 46, 47, 48, 51, 52, 53, 54, 56, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65,65,66,68,69,69 and 69 were dismissed. While dismissing the Writ Petitions, a learned single Judge of the High Court held: (1) that under entry 50 of list II of the 7th schedule to the Constitu tion, the levy was not unconstitutional; (2) that the imposition in question is unreasonably heavy and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner; and (3) that it was discriminatory for a valid classification. The contentions on behalf of the petitioners (1 ) that what fell for consideration before this Court was whether the impugned Rule 21 was invalid as it violated Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The levy in question was constitutionally valid and violative of article 14. [414C] 1(b) A valid classification is a reasonable one. It is well settled that a classification to be valid has to satisfy two conditions: (i) that there is an intelligible differentia between those who are included in the class which is affected by any law or rule and those who arc placed outside the said rule; and and (ii) that each of the peti tioners shall pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. It can be urged before this court that the levy in the instant case was arbitrary and discriminatory for the reason that it relied upon the language of Entry 50 which reads thus: "taxes on mineral rights subject to any limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development" and was, therefore, illegal as it was not in the nature of a fee which could be used either for specific purposes nor for other purposes sanctioned by Law. [408D E] 4(a). By the said decision the validity or constitutionality of such power cannot be judged on the assumption that the executive or the administrative authority acts in an unauthorised manner, its actions would be bad in law and liable to be struck down by the courts but the possibility of abuse of power or arbi trary exercise of discretion cannot invalidate the statute conferring the power or the power which has been conferred by it. [409G H] 5(b).

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the Community of the Sangunathappan Mudaliar Community. The respondents took a different view. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras held that the trusteeship of the appellant was not hereditary. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court which allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam holding that the appellant is a hereditary trustee. In this appeal by certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution, HELD: (i) Section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951 clearly shows that the office of a hereditary trust is in the nature of property. This is so whether the trustee has beneficial interest of some sort or not. [435 D] Amar Das Goswami vs Radhakrishna Das, ; , referred to. (ii) The word 'succession ' in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies passing of an interest from one person to another. [427 E F] In the present case, it was difficult to hold that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy; It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly. [ 426 H] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; followed. (iii)The word 'resuccure ' in section 6( 9) of Act would include even such cases. But the election to the office and of trustee in the present, is for a fixed period of one year and not for life. It is, therefore, difficult to say that there was a succession Of As office of R for a period when on an efflux of time for which S was appointed,. there is no vacancy andB is elected.

The respondents who had a firm of solicitors were partners in a firm. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis and the amount was paid after his death but before he was assessed, they filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and then to the Tribunal. The question was whether the income received subsequent to the previous year in which Amarchand died was liable to be assessed to income tax under section 24B(1) of the Income tax Act for the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. Held, that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section 24 B and cannot be extended beyond that legitimate field. In re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani, , referred to. In the present case the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax were those which were not received in the previous years and were therefore not liable to income of the heirs and legal representatives who cannot be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to these years,.[708 C D] In re. Srelaatsu Areas & Co., Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax Bombay City, , applied. Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd.v. The State of Bihar, [1942] 14 I.T.R. 10, distinguished. In Re Srememati Sehlani Shudhurani and Co. vs The Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay City. ; , at p. 106 it was observed that the question whether a particular amount was income or not had nothing to do with the time of its receipt and the question of receipt was material only for the purposes of determining whether on that amount tax was to be levied under the Act in the year of assessment. The expression 'if he had not died ' means that irrespective of the date of ' receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his heirs his death they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have been liable when the income was received had he been living.

There was no condition as to residence within a State or Union territory prior to the appointment. Under section 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement) Rules, 1959, there is a life of 5 years but by subsequent legislation the period was extended to 10 years. The petitioners who were working in various offices located in different cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad filed writ petitions challenging the validity of the Act which sought to make provision for requirement as to domicile and brought into force on March 21, 1959. The Act was challenged as ultra vires the Constitution. Held: (i) The word 'State ' here is not to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word Article 12 but is not carried to excess by interpretation. The restricted meaning given to a State and Union territory respectively must be viewed narrowly and not carried with excess by construction. The impugned Act has made a declaration that no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory of India because of his residence in any particular part of India. The fact that this clause is an exception and comes into force only once again makes it clear that there can be no discrimination, among other things, on the ground of residence. Realising, however,, that sometimes local Cham sentiments may have to he respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have no significance as the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns or villages. The word "State" here is to be construed in the limited use given by the inclusive clause to expel employment in the State and it means only that. If it chose to speak of residence within parts of State such as District talauqas, talauras, cities etc.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office office. On May 12, 1956, he was searched by the Sub Inspector of Police along with Masood Murtaza Sub Inspector and a shortage of five registered letters and postcards and also the five registered letter in question. At the time of search the appellant who happens to be a trade union official, was not in Bulandshahr but was away on leave at Delhi in connection with a postal conference. The articles were found in an almirah and the key of which was produced by the appellant 's father. On the questions: (1) Whether there is any prejudice as a question of fact and cannot be permitted to be agitated for the first time in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution; (2) whether the prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant; and (3) that, the seizure was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the prosecution had failed to establish that these documents were recovered from the possession of appellant and no presumption can be drawn against him that he had secreted them from his mere fact that they were found at the almirah which, at best, could be regarded as being in the joint possession of himself and his father. There was no evidence that it was ever with the appellant It might not be correct to say that the five letters were secreted by the appel lant 's mother or that there was even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to him would not mean that the articles had ceased to be in course of transmission.

Under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, the Sarpanch and the Pan chas had knowledge of the order. The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and even if a Panchas had knowledge that the District Magistrate was not satisfied for want of evidence by way of proper affidavit etc., the Nyaya Panchayat had rightly dismissed the application. On appeal to this Court it was contended : (i) that the procedure adopted by the Gram panchs in not doing so was really not bona fide; (ii) that even if the Panchas did not believe the contents of the application, and affidavit of the party that the High Court had stayed further proceedings before the Panchayat, nor was there any thing in the order sheet to show that the Panchas did not belief he bad the contents. HELD : (1) Where a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of contempt of court for disobeying the order.[119 C E] (2)(a) The High court 's finding that the Sarpanch had knowledge over the copy of the telegram was not recorded and only copy of an telegram was produced. It was no part of the duty of the Pan COcha to enquire from the S.D.M about the filing of the original application before him. At any rate, he has apparently no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before them when no proceeding is pending before him.[119 E F] (b) There is no such evidence in this case. [119 F G] (d) It is not proved on record that any such application was made by the Sarpanch to the Gram Panchs of the Panchayat which was merely an affidavit sworn to before a person authorised to administer oaths. It be true that in some cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of Court.[120 E F G].

The appellant was tried along with the other co accused for causing the death of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge, Etawah convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced him to imprisonment till life. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) There is no enmity between Ujagar Singh and the appellant against whom the extra judicial confession was made had no motive to harm Sheo Sahai and he had purchased a sword from the deceased; (ii) there was a quarrel in a play of cards, that the appellant did commit murder of Sheo Narain; and (iii) there were good reasons for Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai, and that he did not place any reliance on his statement which was supported by Paley Singh. [207 E G] (a) There was no reason to think that the extrajudicial confession of the appellant to Ujagar Singh finds ample support from the facts that the appel lant did purchase a sword day before, that very sword was found to be stained with human blood immediately after his murder and that sword was handed over by the appellant himself to the Police Officer at the Police Station. [206 E] (b) The extra judicial confessions, therefore, could not be said to have been made by the appe lant to Ujagar singh or consequently we do not place reliance on this extrajudicial confessional confession. [205 F G] In the instant case, it was not a matter of surprise that he along with other co ties meetings the appellant and others told the people of what they had been informed by the appellants. It was not therefore a matter in which it could be said that the statements made by Patey Singh, P.W. 2, who states that the Sub Inspector was not present when Ujagar Singh related to them the fact which had taken place at night and by Bishram Singh,P.W . 13, who deposed that Ujagar Singh stated that he was taking his bath at night in the Canal from the depradations of neel gais. They also knew what they said were told by the accused, and not what they did actually told them. [208 E F] (c) It is unnecessary to decide whether any portion of the report dictated by the SubInspector at the police station was admissible or not in evidence as there was good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on by the High Court. The extrajudicial confessions, however, could be considered not to have made a statement when the appellant had himself proceeds to the police Station and hands over the blood stained sword.

The second respondent published a preliminary electoral roll on September 30, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 (the Act). The Returning officer published the preliminary electoral rolls under r. 8 of the Rules and after notices to all persons whose names had not been included in the electoral roll submitted their claims and/or objections within 20 days from the date of publication of the said notice. In the election petition filed by one of the defeated candidates, the second respondent, who was the petitioner in the earlier writ petition, claimed to be included in his constituency on October 19, 1978 and that he had filed a claim to include his name in the Electoral Roll on October 20, 1978 which was rejected by the Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. The petitioners alleged that there was an error in the notice issued under r.(I) of Rule 4 of the rules requiring that claims and objections should be preferred within 30 days from tho date of the publication of that notice and for the second time that, the applications were disposed of on October 31, 1978. On December 30,1978, the first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court praying for quashing the electoral rolls and the calendar of events issued for the purposes of the election and directing the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31,1978. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding (i) that the second petitioner was not prompt in moving the High court, and that the writ Petition itself was presented on December 27, 1978; (ii) that a large number or people who could have filed claims and claims had, objected to the inclusion of his name therein in the elec tion roll on October 1, 1978, and (iii) that none of the persons mentioned in Annexure P 7 preferred any claim before respondent No. 2 on October 21, 1978 or on any other sub sequent date. The respondents moved a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court and a Division Bench dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners were not prompt to move the High Courts after undue delay. The appellant company, its directors, filed a complaint and made certain statements in an application before the Registrar of Companies for failure to Me with the Registrar. The respondent company, as also its directors on or before 30 101967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account had not been laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid. The High Court, taking the view that a person charged with an offence cannot rely on his default as an answer to the charge and so if he was responsible for not calling the general meeting, rejected the complaint, holding it to have committed the default in complying with the provisions of section 220(1) of the Companies Act, 1913, and, in appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal ^ HELD: The High Courts have considered this question after the decision of this Court in the State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani and Others ; , that a company or its directors in a prosecution under section 32 and section 133 of the (new) Companies Act cannot rely upon their failure to call the general body meet as a defence to the prosecution. [416C] The words "were so laid" make the filing of copies of those balance sheets and profit & loss account before the company at such meeting a duly approved and audited balance sheet. The failure to do so would not be a compliance with the provision of the section. The provisions unmistakably indicate, as we said earlier, that the holding of the annual general meeting and the lay before it of the balance sheets are a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the printer body meeting in an essential prerequisite. If no such general body meetings is held, it is obvious that no copies of the entire balance sheet (1) A.I.R. 1969 Orissa 234 (5) A I.T.R, 1947 Madras 44 and profit or loss account can be sent to the Registrar even without the necessity of their being laid before the general Body meeting of the company. [417E F] Further, on principle and authority it should be held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134. They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section134. The view taken by this Court is correct. Under the provisions emerges as a general law for the regulation of the affairs of the Company, the carrying on of business at any time was incidental to their business. Section 131 is limited to the preparation of a list of members of the general company and of persons who have ceased to be members of a general company. Under section 133, the failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable. But if no balance sheet is laid before it, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balancesheet and to the copies thereafter required to be filed with the Committee. If the requirements of sub section (2) of section 134 are not complied with even then, the persons concerned would be liable for punishment for that default. [414E F; 415G H] Further in construing a penal provision it is not permissible to give an extended meaning to the plain words of the Section on the ground that a principle recognised in respect of certain other provisions of law requires that this section should be interpreted is the same way. The court there observed that the decision in Park vs Lawton (supra) will not apply.

The respondent was charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by him in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as Jessop Factory at Dum Dum and it was found that the factory was just closed, that the workers employed therein were not allowed to work in any part of the factory for a few days they went out to take down the atmosphere of working and that they had asked them to work for some time for doing so but there was no answer from their employer. The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, which provided that "A Special Court shall try such offences or classes of cases or classes off racing offences or cases or class of cases as may be in its judgment require speedier trial. The High Court quashed the conviction on the grounds: (i) section 5(1) was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion inasmuch as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right to equality guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of that 's freedom under article 301 of the Constitution, in so far as it conferred arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case; (ii) section 269 (1), was discriminatory inasmuch as even if any unguided power had been conferred on the executive by the statute itself cannot be said to have violated the equality clause though questions relating to proper exercise of such power or the limits of delegation might arise. Held, (per C.J., P. Hayaji and K. Das JJ.), that the classification contemplated in section 5 was not arbitrary but must be reasonable and rational, that is to say it was based on a reasonable classification of persons to whom or the offences in respect of which procedure laid down in it was to apply and hence it was necessary to ascertain whether it was actually based on such a classification. A distinction made between cases and offences triable by special courts and those by ordinary courts must be distinguished from other cases and not just one of fact. The classification must not be arbitrary but should be rational, because it must not only be based on some intelligible differentia which distinguishes altogether from others and not in others who are left out but those qualities or characteristics must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation.

The appellant was appointed as a lecturer in Radiology in Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. By an order dated January 14, 1963 the Central Health Service was reorganized with effect from September 9, 1966 and the concept of General Duty Officers and Specialist Grade Officers was introduced for the first time. Under r. 4 (2) every vacancy in the Specialists ' Grade shall be filled by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the post in the senior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that scale and 20% of the vacancies thereof were to be filled up by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second Schedule. On January 14 1963 the appellant was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview on August 7, 1972 for the post of Professor of Radiotherapy but since the post was falling vacant in 1973 he did not appear for the interview. The Government of India Ministry of Health & Family Planning informed the Principal that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the post because the teaching experience gained by him while holding the Post of Radiologist cum Associate Professor from the other subjects of radiology (ex officio) cannot be taken into consideration for determining his eligibility for appointment as Professor or Radiology. The Ministry of Finance by its letter dated January 17, 1976 informed the Delhi Administration that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital and if he wanted to join as Professor of radiotherapy (exinagar Kalra) in the Medical College. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated December 12, 1964 as also the order of acquisition passed by the Government of Punjab under section 3(2A). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that though the appellant had the essential qualification prescribed for teaching post the teaching work gained by the appellant while holding that the post could not he taken into account for determining the question of his eligibility, for appointment, as Professor/ Radiologist or Radiological (exclusively) in Ma Gurudwara Medical College because the Teaching experience gained was akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor in that College. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondents that since the appellant did not hold the post he was not eligible for appointment under r. 8(2 A), and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second schedule he was clearly eligible for his appointment as Associate Professor. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The determination of the question whether a Specialist grade II in a teaching hospital belonging to the Central Government Health Service is eligible for consideration for promotion or appointment cannot depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellant firm had been carrying on a business on April 1, 1939 from before and for the years 1948 49. The income tax Officer rejected its claim alleging that there was discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 25(3) read with section 25 (4). At the instance of the partners the Appellate Assistant Commissioner referred the question to the High Court which answered in favour of the assessee by holding that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 25A(4), because, as in the earlier case the business had been discontinued on April1 1939, it could not be said that there new business was carried on by a firm. Thereupon the three partners filed appeals before the Tribunal. The Tribunal took the view that the partnership mentioned in annexure C I was different from the partnership which was brought about by the instrument of December 6, 1918 and consequently it couldnot have been carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, that the income, profits and gains of the previous year should be deemed to have been the income. The High Court held that the business in soap and umbrella was different as from the business of banking and piece goods and yarn and that the amalgamation of these two businesses amounted to a succession by a newly constituted firm. Held: (1) The partnership mentioned therein in annexure D I was distinct from the original partnership which had been brought about, and it was not in terms of joint family business but in terms Of business in a business sense and it is the business which was taxed under the Act of 1918 which must cease to exist before the benefit of section 24(4) can be obtained. (2) The High Courts were right in holding that a mere change in the constitution of the partnership does not count and sections 25(4)(a), 26(3), 26, 25(1), 26 and 26(2) do not apply at the same time because there is no cessation of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned. (3) The income derived from the appellant firm by way of tax which alone had paid tax under the Income Tax Act 1918 could be held to be property within section 25B(4).

Section 5(1) of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, provides that no person shall be entitled to inspect, call for, or obtain copies of any documents, statement or papers or materials furnished to him which he considers necessary and obtain from another person or banking or other company. The procedure thus prescribed in sub section (4) of section 5 is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed under the Indian Income tax Act. Therefore, when the Commission is collecting the materials from different sources against the assessee appellant he is not entitled to be present at those stages and take part in the enquiry but after a material is ready and placed on the record then he can be present and has to be given a reasonable opportunity of rebutting any evidence that may have been collected against him. The latter procedure thus followed by the Commission was contained in section 7 which provided that "no person shall lie or, unless he is an authorised official, make enquiries in such manner as it or he may deem fit and obtain copies from such person or bank statements on oath or otherwise on such points or any matter as may be specified". The Central Government referred these cases to the Commission for investigation. On the 15th of September 1953, a report was made by the Registrar of the Commission that the case of the petitioner along with the cases of Suraj Mall Mohta and other members of his family may be referred to the (Commission) for investigation, and report any case or points in a case, which the Central Government had prima facie reasons for believing that a person had evaded payment of tax on income together with such material as may he available in support of such belief, and that the Central Govern ment was bound to refer their cases to an advisory committee and that it would be sufficient if the Commission were to do so. The Commission submitted its report. On receipt of the report the Central Govt. referred these case to the Investigation Commission under the provisions of section 561(4) and they were numbered 831/64 69 on the records of the commission. The Commis sioner thereupon notified two persons that their cases had been referred for investigation and they had been called upon to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure 'B ' of the petition, to the Com missioner under section 5(4). The petitioners challenged the validity of these provisions on the ground that: (i) the provisions Of sections 5( 1), 5(2), 6, 7 and 8 of the Act had become void as being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the Constitution; (ii) the procedure to be followed by it was inconsistent with article 14 of the Constitu tion and infringed articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31(2); and (iii) the proviso to section 5 of the , which empowered a Commission to require any person or any banking or another company to prepare and furnish on or before a specified date written statements of accounts; Held, (per Das ), that sections 5 (4), 6 and 8 Of the Indian Incometax Act do not offend article 14 Of the Constitution. What section 5 (1) acts is not merely a wide power but is a part of it in terms, and where an investigation has been started under this Act, the matter should be referred for finding out whether that section amounts to denial of equal protection of laws, the provision being reasonable must be complied with. It was not correct to say that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and do not truly disclose all particulars or material facts necessary for their assessment and against whom a report is made under section 6 (4).

The appellant, a saw mill of the Company was in the employ of one of its workmen and was threatened with physical violence. He was caught hold by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on the Company which had asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. He thus committed no misconduct as he did not serve any department or employees in general. His dismissal order was set aside by the Tribunal but the Tribunal held that though something seemed to have happened, on the afternoon of June 21, 1958, it could not come to the conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or other officers. In appeal before this Court, HELD: (1) The Industrial Court was right in holding that the exercise of power in this case was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of its power under the rule in as much as that rule was used to get rid of an employee instead of following the course of holding an inquiry for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. [827E] (2) A provision like r. 18(a) is in these terms: "When the management desires to determine the services of any permanent workmen receiving 12 as wages, otherwise than under rule 21, he shall be given 14 days notice or pay 12 days wages. " It may be mentioned that r. 21 deals with cases of misconduct and provides for dismissal or suspension for misconduct and in such a case the workman so suspended is not entitled to any wages during the period of suspension. The claim thus put forward on behalf of the appellant cannot be accepted and it was too late in the day for an employer to raise such a claim for it amounts to a claim "to hire and fire" an employee as the employer pleases and thus completely negatives security of service which has been secured to industrial employees through industrial adjudication for over a long period of time now. [825F G] (3) It is well settled that if an employer wanted to take action for misconduct under r.18(a), it is now well settled in view of the decisions of this Court in Parshotam Lal Dhingra vs Union of India, ; , and Mahar Oil Company vs Its Workmen, [1962] I S.C.R. 202, that a workman who has acted under that rule must have unfettered right "to hiring and fire". that right is now subject to industrial adjudication and even a power like that granted by r. 12(a). Therefore the employer could defend his action under r, 18(c) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action taken under that r should be bona fide. [826C] (4) The question whether an employee can defend the action under R. 18 (a) or say that having acted under the Rule there was nothing more to be said and the Industrial Court could inquire into the causes that led to the termination of service under R '18(c). Since it was not accepted by industrial tribunals over a Long course of years, it cannot be said that it was incorrect.

The respondents were the owners of a theatre. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Faraqui on the one hand, right to exhibit cinematograph films was granted to the latter on certain terms and conditions to two persons, namely, Rasiklal, Bhai Nabeer Hussain Khan Tejabwala, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibited any picture in contravention of the terms and cond ion of the agreement dated October 27,1954. At the hearing and the evidence of a representative of Filmistan Distributors (India) Private Ltd., (Filmistan 's Association) had been recorded, counsel for the defendants asked in cross examination the question whether the said document was a lease. The trial Judge passed an order disallowing the objection and dismissed the suit. At this stage the plaintiff filed a revision application against that order before the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was allowed on a number of points, but granted fresh and additional written statements to support the issues raised by the defendants. By a subsequent order of the High court allowing the revision petition, the High Curt held that the question asked in the cross examination could not be excluded. The plaintiff then filed an appeal under section 116 of the Civil Procedure Code, challenging the correctness of the findings of the trial Court on issues Nos. 11, 12 and 13 as preliminary issues. On a reference by the High COurt, the question was, whether in view of the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 defendants Nos. 5 and 6 were estopped from contending and leading any evidence and putting questions in cross examina tion of plaintiffs witnesses to show that the said agreement dated December 1, 1960 created a lease and that the consent decrees operated as res judicata. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the defendants that an enquiry into the nature of legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to be put to the witnesses for Filmistans, and that having regard to the terms of the said consent decree as also the fact that the suit had not been even averred in the plaint in that suit it was not even averred that the rights granted were in the nature o lease.f November 27 1954, that in the earlier suit it had not even whispered that it was a leasing, and hence the suit was for declaration of the rights of Films under the agreement. Allowing the appeal, HELD : The language of section 115 Code of civil Procedure is derived from the section 28 of the Act but at the same time if an issue Is in fact barred by res judicata then the Court has no jurisdiction on principles of res judicata to go into that question or to decide that question over again to the extent to which the court, viz., the trial court in the instant case, proposed to go to that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1. 1960 to be reopened, it is proposing to exercise the jurisdiction which is not vested in it by law.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The Sessions Judge acquitted the accused but convicted him under section 307 Indian Penal Code. In appeal, in revision to the High Court, the appellant reiterated his plea that there was no reason to doubt the testimony of the prosecution witnesses which was supported by the medical evidence. He urged (i) that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and they had been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge; (ii) that there could be no reason for doubt the reliability of the evidence; (iii) that where two views of the witnesses are possible, the accused is entitled to the benefit of the doubt arising from the two views and that where the Trial Court has taken a possible view and acquitted the appellant, the High court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view was also possible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(i) The principles are now well settled. At one time it was thou ht that an order of acquitting could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial", and invite conclusions. However, the 'formula ' of "substantial & compelling reasons ' and the search for them were abandoned as a result of the pronouncement of this Court in Sanwat Singh 's case. Occasionally phrases like 'manifestly illegal ', grossly unjust ' have been used to describe the orders of acquittal which warrant interference. But it is essential that any view of the Evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable even as any doubt, the benefit Of which an accused person may claim, must be a reasonable doubt. [368 G H] Sanwat vs Minister of pensions, ; , followed. 1096 (ii)(a) An order of discharge could be interfered with only where two substantial and compelling grounds out of conviction are possible. The principles laid down in San wat Singh ' 's Case may be added the further principle that "if two reasonable conclusions can be reached on the basis of the evi dence on record, the Appellate Court should not disturb the finding of the Trial court". [368 F G] Sanawat Singh & Ors. vs State of U.P., A.l. R. 1959 S.C., 460, applied.

% The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was prosecuted for having committed offences under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. He was in possession of pecuniary resources disproportionate to his known sources of income. It was alleged that he had incurred certain criminal activities during the period from September 1961 till November 1966 and during the service tenure, he used financial resources. The sanction order stated that the accused would be immune from prosecution for anything connected with his business. The charge against him was that he was holding various pecuniary resources with an intention of preventing him from discharging his official duties and that he must have earned or realizable wealth for over 35 years. He had to pay Rs. 500/ as loans in excess of the loan granted by him, and also a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs towards interest on certain dates. The prosecution alleged that after the suit was filed in this Court, the High Court appointed the Judge of a High Court as well as Shri R.S. Pathak, Chief Justice to hold the office of Judge for some time and on his recommendation, Shri R once again promoted him as Additional Chief Secretary to the Government, who had been given permission to conduct the inquiry, etc., and made available the records of the case. The Judge ultimately held that the Judge was not competent to remove a Judge either of the Judges or of the High Courts from his office unless he issued a warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India. He accordingly convicted him for contravening section 5 (1) (c) punishable by an order dated January 17, 1978 made under Section 5(2) of that Act on September 25, 1979. Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no power to review its own orders and substitute its own views. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of review vested in the Supreme judiciary is a legislative one. [258F] 1.2 The power conferred by Article 121 of the Constitution can be exercised only if after the requisite sanction under Section 6 has been obtained it becomes necessary to consider the feasibility of grant of sanction under section 6 and that the holder of an office who may be a public servant according to the wide definition of expression in the Act but whose category for the grant of such sanction for prosecution is not envisaged by Section 6 of the Act, is outside the purview of the provi sions as enjoined by Section 5 (3) of Article 124. [259G] 1:3 The word 'public servant ' has been defined in Section 2(g) to mean a person who has at any time during the tenure of office, been in possession for which his public servant cannot satisfactorily account. Blackbehari Singh vs State of Punjab, ; at p. 264, followed. In other words, if the holder or of a public office during his tenure in office cannot be prosecuted without sanction under Sections 6 and 5 (2) then, as held in Antulay, no sanction for his prosecution after ceasing to hold office may be neces sary, but his prosecution is made because while in office he could be prosecuted with the previous sanction under sections 6 and 7 of the . [262D E] 1 :4 In the case of Judges of the high Court and the Supreme Courts there is no such requirement under any provi section of furnishing particulars of their assets so as to provide a record thereof with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is nothing repugnant in the subject or context. [263D E; 264A B] 2.1 Even after the 1964 amendment of the provisions of Article 122 (5) read with Article 124(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with the office.

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Sahas secured 16,730 votes and Sudhir secured 15,523 and the former was declared elected. Sudhir then filed a petition challenging the validity of the election on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal, however he challenged the validity only on the ground that, as Abhokoy Pa was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Caste group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas and the appellant 's case was that the appellant belonged to the Scheduled Castes. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. An appeal against the decision of the Tribunal in favour of Sudhir, was preferred to the Patna High Court and the question for consideration related to the interpretation of the item was whether the appellant satisfied the description " Sunri excluding Saha" in item 40 of the President 's order. The appellant contended: (1) that he was a reserved caste by birth but was not excluded from his Scheduled Caste because he belongs to a larger class group of spouses known as a group of Redis or not and therefore was not a member thereof; (2) that the expression "excluding Saha" meant excluding Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri is a caste group ; (3) that it indicates men of the Sunri caste but not those within that caste who formed the smaller caste groups of Sahas. HELD: (i) The contention that the word "included in item40 must be understood as referring to a bigger caste group under the Sunmi caste was irrelevant and therefore did not apply to the case, [390D] (ii) Item 40 of Part 13 of Schedule to the Order which set out which were Scheduled Castes in West Bengal stood as follows: "Sunri excluding" Sahas: phrase shall be deleted from the word ' RANGN '. The Tribunal came to its conclusion that the Sahas formed a distinct caste wholly outside the Suniti caste and they had been specifically excluded in item 39 for the greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin. [390 E G] (iii)The Tribunal was therefore right in construing the item on the evidence in the case as they appeared to have done.

The assessee, a public limited company, filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49 which was the previous calendar year and was the assessment years 1950 51. The Income Tax Officer determined assessable profits to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore State and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Indian Income tax Act the loss received in Travancore state should be taken into account for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purposes of determining income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that State. The assessee 's appeals were unsuccessful but the Tribunal held that a set off under section 24(1), proviso (1) must be preferred in respect of all the questions raised by the revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i)(a) Under the Travancore Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, the words " British India or in an Indian State" have to be substituted. A proviso cannot be construed as enlarging the scope of a provision when it can be fairly and properly construed without attributing to it that effect. It was not correct to say that business in section 10 means business in British India and business in an I.T.R. in which case only need recourse be had to section 24, sub section (1). [260 A B] The Indian Income Tax Amendment Act, 19 of 1941 does not distinguish between business in the two territories. But then it was said that as the profits or gains of business in a British India are exempted from payment of income tax unless received or brought into British India there is no positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business" and compel the application of the proviso to the same head, specially keeping in view the object of the main section. [261 G]. (b) The use of these words does not circumscribe the proviso lo the profits and losses arising under the head business in two territories, i. e., British India & the Indian States. [260 C] (c) In sections 2(13), 14(2)(e) and 6 of the Travancore Act of 1918 corresponding to section 34, the word used was ' income which in the latter Act was expanded into " income, profits and gains ". The mere fact that the word " income" is not used does not justify the construction.

The first respondent company was a Private Limited Company to take over the business of its partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co. which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July, 1947, an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees at Calcutta under which, the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. Subsequently, in September 1959, an arbitration award was passed fixing the age at 60 but the appellant Company challenged that award before the Industrial Tribunal by means of a writ petition. Thereafter the company resisted the workmen 's claim and contended that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had earlier been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age 60 subject to employees passing medical examination at reaching the 55 subject to their employee passing a Medical Examination on reaching an age of 55. The Tribunal held that this Court refused to disturb the award fixing the period of retirement at 60 years and, therefore, did not disturb the order fixing the retirement age at sixty60. It further directed that the age for workmen who were represented was fixed at 60 then, but the company could in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was entirely on the industry cum region basis. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The award and agreements on the question of age of superannuation about which information is furnished by several documents on this record clearly show a consistent trend in the Bombay region to fix the retirement Age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 60. This was reasonable and unambiguous and they must be reasonably relied upon, namely, the observations made by this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs The Workmen ; , and Dunzmellop Rubber Company Ltd.,v. workmen and others; [427 E F] (ii) In spite of these infirmities the Tribunal took into account the fact that the Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix its retirement age on 60 years, but had brushed them aside in a way for which, on a closer examination it was clear that this document was of little assistance for finding out the recent trend. [427 C] (iii) The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this court in appeal, was erroneous on the whole unsound. If this Court had erred in making those pronouncements it would be the first to admit such mistakes and to correct the error. After careful consideration of all the materials placed on record, we have found nothing to justify any doubt about the correctness of what was stated on the earlier occasion. [435 E G] (iv) The Tribunal was right in holding that questions which could justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an experi mental occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous. The Court did not notice any slowing down of this trend. That is why an award can be revised or altered to correct to correct it.

The first respondent company was the managing director of a Barium Chemicals Ltd. and was at the relevant time one Minister to Finance in the Government of India, but it had been appointed under that power with the consent of the Central Government. The second respondent was also acting as Chairman for a period of two years from June 4, 1965 to July 9, 1964. In April 1952, the first respondent passed an order framing charges against the first appellant company and after due notice, issued by the Board on August 5, 1965, he was prosecuted in the Court of the Judicial Magistrate under section 237(b) of the , for having acted mala fide, without jurisdiction as required by sub section (4A) added subsequently. He challenged the validity of the order as being mala fide and without jurisdiction, contending that the provisions of section 237 (b) were void and without prejudice to his rights guaranteed under article 19(1)(g) of 'the Constitution. Held, that the second respondent had clearly stated that there was ample material before the Board to form the opinion that there were circumstances suggesting the existence of one or more of the matters in sub cls. (i), (ii), and (iii) of section 10E. The action was bad as mala fide because not the Board but the Chairman alone acted, as mala fides because no honest opinion was formed on the matter which under the section give rise to the power but on irrelevant and extraneous material, and further because the order was passed under the influence and malice of a Minister who was interested in another company belonging to his sons and sought this means to oust a rival. Held further, that as soon as may be after the commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Act 1963, the Central Govern ment has power to constitute the Company law Board, it is not competent merely to do so and there are circumstances suggesting that fraud and other kinds of mismanagement mentioned in sub cl. (ii) would make it obligatory on such a member to give information relating to the calculation of the commission payable to a managing or other director, the managing agent, the secretaries etc., if any, as may he specified in the order, such of its powers and functions as it may think fit; and every order made or act done in the exercise of this power or discharge of such functions shall be deemed to be the orders or acts as the case may be, of the Board. Under section 237 of the Indian , the Central Govt. may, by notification in the Official gazette constitute a Company Law Board to exercise and discharge such powers and duties conferred on it by or under this Act or any other law, as might be delegated to it by that Government. There is also ample material to show that fraud, intent to defraud or misconduct was followed by the Directors even though they may not have been considered. The directors were appointed for two years. Although powers were vested in the Board as Chairman and the Board had no power to authorise the Chairman to sub delegate such functions to himself and consequently, the company Law Board (Procedure) Rules, 1964 made by the Central Goverment on February 1, 1964 and the Chairman 's order delegating the function of the board under section 239 to the Chairman are ultra vires the and the impugned order is invalid. Not only the Board could pass an order under section 240, a case similar to that of an exceptional kind was made out in the present case, where powers were given by two different authorities, the same authority had been exercised on irrelevant materials, the scheme and object of the Act could not be challenged but distinguished.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced under section 395 I.P.C. for the murder of certain cotton pieces from two carts within the limits of Lingsugar Police Station at about 1130 P.m. The facts are that one traders in cloth sent their wares in carts for sale. The cartmen halted after the market was over on the way for food. Thereafter six carts left for Mudgal at about 10 p.m., 20 persons were said to have approached the carts and pelted stones. It is not necessary to go into rest of the case or the evidence on which the case of dacoity was established, because dacoity as such was not challenged before us, on the sole evidence of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to the traders. The appellants contended that they could be suspected to be dacoits and convicted accordingly under section 396 I. P.C., but not of complicity in the crime of dacoity. HELD : There was no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against the appellants. Although there is some other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of stolen property with him was a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. [724G H] It must not be forgotton that the offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons or more. The houses of 20 persons are searched and large quantities of the stolen goods were found in their houses. It may be 723 impossible to think that these 20 persons accused were merely receivers of stolen properties from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits. Therefore, a sentence of three years ' rigorous imprisonment will meet.

The petitioners were found manufacturing a commodity with some other substance. The Act was enacted to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons and the importation of the same. In pursuance of this power by the Notification No. F 10/44/72 fin i. G) dated 7th August, 1973 the Lt. Governor amended the Delhi Poisons Rules, 1926 by including to the list of substances included in the Rules as "Poisons" "the substance commonly known as 'thinner ' containing spirit and other soluble material such as shellacin in which the percentage of such soluper di rect material does not exceed 30% as poison and consequential amendment of rules 12 and 13 of the Rules. The petitioners contended that inasmuch as the Act was a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory treatment as it was left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison. Dismissing the Writ Petition, HELD: 1.1. The provisions of both sections 2 and 5 are not hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223B] 1.2. It is now well settled that a law in force in the territory of India before the commencement of the Constitution is altered and re enacted as Poison Act 12 of 1919 the definition was omitted and speci fied substances were included in that schedule with a power vested in the State Government by law to amend the same by Rules including other substances to the Lists of po divisions. [222C E] 1:3. The provision of neither section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by Article 14 of the Consti tration Limitation Act. [221F G] 1 :4. In the instant case, the provisions of either sections 2 or 5 and the impugned Notification are hit under article 14. The writ petition accordingly fails and it is dismissed.
