The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of two districts, namely, (1) presided officers of district courts, (2) the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, and (3) the District and Sessions judge of Ganjam district and sessions judge. The former consists of eight district and Session judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges. All these officers are the members of a joint cadre consisting comprising of nine district, and sessions judges, secretary to Government in law department. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar is exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Court as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The power to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. It appears that for some time past there were differences between the High court and the Government about the posting of some judicial officers. The High Court took the view that those officers had no authority to hold the posts they were holding. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the order of the High 'Court is liable to be set aside as it casts duty upon the Government to abide by any statutory instructions in the matter and after taking into consideration its recommendations should have been implemented by the State Government; and (ii) that that since the rule laid down in Ranga Mahammad vs State of West Bengal was not followed, it vitiated the order. Dismissing the appeals HELD: (i)(i) The High ' Court must be held to have had that right as those posts were included in the cadre of superior judicial service. [161 A] (ii)(a) The power of transfer of District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the Cadre must necessarily be outside the power of the Governor and fall under the control vested in it by article 235.

Section 15 of the, 1913 Act as it originally stood underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as amended read as under: "15. Persons in whom right of pre emption vests in respect of sales of agricultural land and village immovable property shall vest (a) where the sale is by a sole onwer First, in the son or daughter or son 's son or grandson 's sons of the vendor or vendors; (b) wherethe sale is of a share out of joint land or property and is not made by all the co sharers jointly, only the other co shar ers and the tenants can exercise the right of preemption. " In 1978, section 15 of 1913 Act came into force in Haryana which had replaced the Act in 1973 but it stood later became part of the State of Punjab. Section 15 of that Act as amended by 1913 Act provided for pre emptment to co sharer in relation to Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution which was challenged on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 15 of The trial court rejected the contention of the appellant that the interpretation placed by the two judge Bench on the expression 'other co sharmers ' in section 15(1) (b), amounts to discrimination on the basis that if an outsider was introduced as a co sharner in a property it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. The courts below found, however, that what was said about the right Of pre emution vested in a tenant was upheld on the con tention that if a outsider is introduced as co shar er in a lated property it would make common relicing more difficult and destroyed the benefits which were conferred on him by that provision. The High Court also held that the view of the two Judge Bench on that point was correct, the interpretation relied upon by the three judge Bench of this Court in the case of Anantha Rao vs State of Karnataka & Ors. , ; , must be upheld. Allowing the appeal by certificate to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The exercise of the right owes statutorily fixed and even thereafter in the first three clauses of section 15 (1)(b) may or may not be co shar eders. [123C] 2. It is difficult to hold that this Court intended to deny the right to pre em pption of those kinsfolk even if they happened to be co owners. That would clearly be discriminatory and violative of Articles 14, 15 and 16 of the Constitu tion.

The appellant, who was a widow and son of the respondent, had instituted a suit for title and injunction in respect of the property which constitutes the subject matter of dispute to third parties. The appellant claimed that she had paid Rs. 1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The alienees have spent considerable amount of money towards sale of the said property which was more than three years old by now. This fact has been admitted in the litigation. Respondent No. 2 filed a suit to enforce the mortgage decree on the ground that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise and it was not binding. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the transfer of the appellant with respect of property which became the subject mater of dispute was valid under the compromise deed. In appeal the High Court held that once the court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the court to act otherwise. Hence this appeal by the alienees. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The alienations are for about a purported consideration of Rs. 4 lakhs. The sale deeds indicate that a sum of Rs,.1 lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. The High Court was in error in holding that once on the Court was satisfied, there was no compromise it could be for the court lo act otherwise [543 G] 2. If the compromise petition is valid and lawful the same has to be acted upon. [541 B C] 3. When the matter was listed before the Court for recording of a compromise, the alienee had disputed the fact of payment and had, in the meantime alienated about 81 acres of property and which constituted the subject ' matter of controversy to third party. The transferees have admittedly been in possession of the properties from the date of the sales which is more than 3 years old. [543 E G] 4. The alienation deeds are for Rs.1 lakh and Rs.77,124. Out of the price paid during the pendency of the special leave petition no amount had been paid earlier and the net amount has not been able to point out any justification as to why the compromise should not be acted on and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. [542 G] 5. The appellants have already been brought on record under order of this Court. Though there was the allegation that some improvements had been made to the property in the property prior to 21, there is no justification as regards to why it should not he acted upon and on that basis on the foundation of it, the litigation might not be dispose of. The factum of compromise is not in dispute. Respondent Nos. 2 and his counsel have accepted the fact that the parties have signed the compromise petitions which contain terms which they had accepted and all parties have accepted, the document of compromise to be genuine. Counsel for the alienors has taken the stand that the said alienations are valid and the transferees have become owners of the Property and have even maintained that there have been improvements of the land by the vendees. He sought to rely on certain decisions which were referred to in the decision, [543 B] 6. The assignees have already filed an attempt to hold out that there are disputes about a con tract for sale Prior to 21.8.1987 and it is not binding since they had no interest in the properties prior to it. They have not been paid. There was, therefore, no order for costs.

In Appeals Nos. 51 and 52 of 1975 filed by the workmen (in CA No. 1951/75) dated 30th July, 1974, challenging the award of the Industrial Tribunal, Gujarat on September 24, 1975 in the dispute between the Company and its workmen, the questions that arise for consideration were whether the benefits admissible under the Act in Baroda should be granted to the workmen under the available provisions of the , and what has been awarded by the Tribunal is additional privilege leave for 7 days in the garb of sick leave. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Scheme of the benefits ador quo ante cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Industrial Court. [83 E] 2.1 It cannot be contended that the benefit should not be admissible on the ground that it had not been allowed by other companies in the region. The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and has given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of 7 days sick leave in the manner set out in the award. [86 F] 2:2. In providing for periodical payment to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the reasoning of sickness. [85G] 2 :3 The amounts awarded by Tribunal are not similar to those admissible under enactments. In view of the provisions of s.41 and 42 of the an unreported award, it is apparent that the claim for grant of sick Leave can be decided on merits. Secondly, it would be open to the Tribunal to examine the demand in respect of sickness benefit claimed by the company.

The appellant who was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay, was arrested on the 24th August, 1954 and is in detention since then under the impugned order the grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of detention. The validity of the order was challenged on the following grounds: (a) There was a sudden search by the police on the 26th August. at the appellant 's place for alleged possession of illicit liquor; and (b) there was a possibility of his being allowed to make a representation under article 22(5). Held, that the order passed by the detaining authority was not based upon any real application of mind by the respondent. The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars under article 8(6) covers both these elements and therefore it could not be said that he applied for the purpose of disclosing a ground which would enable him to make such representation, and so as to nullify the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in those circumstances. The obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feels he need not have felt that the grounds furnished were so vague as to hamper him in his right to make representation under Article 22(6). On reading the grounds it was clear that the appellant himself did not appear to have felt any of these points and there is nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the Slate authority at the time when the grounds were furnished.

The Central Government directed removal from service of ten respondents under r. 14, the Army Rules, 1954. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court contending that r.14 was ultra vires the . The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order removing the respondent from service on the ground that r 14 was ultra rites. On appeal by special leave the Union of India contended: (i) Whether r. 17, made under section 19 is ultra vires; (ii) Whether it is ultra rites the petitioner has no case. The Army Rules 1954, including r. 12, were framed in exe cise of the powers conferred by section 191 of the . Rule 14 of the Army Rule, 1954 is not ultra vires. In order to give power to the Central Government to remove an officer without being tried and convicted by court martial under section 191, it follows that there must be rules, and subject to the provisions of the Act and such rules, the Central Govt may dismiss or remove him from the service; and (iii) in the event of the explanation of the officer being considered unsatisfactory by the "C in C, or when so directed by the Central Govern ment, the case shall be submitted to the C government with the officer 's defence The rule is not therefore ultra vires as it was contended that the words "subject to the section of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes s.19 subject to section 45, and the Central Goverment has thus no power to remove a person from the serv ice in derogation of the provisions Of section 45.

The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of the imposition of octroi duty. It was contended that the procedure prescribed by rr.3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi limits were fixed on January 14, 1964; (1) that r. 23 which provided for appeals in these terms was ultra vires, and (2) that under r. 21 the appellants were not importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale. Held: The levy of octroi from January 14 to April 1, 1963 was regularised in accordance with law. Sec. 167(3)(b) entrusted the expression "any person aggrieved by the assessment, levy or imposition of any tax or fee" in r. 5 read with r.21 and is headed "Appeal against levy of any such tax or fees". Rule 20 provides that no appeal shall lie to Panchayat Samiti. The scheme of the Fees Rules was first to prescribe general rules and then to deal individually with various taxes. Under r. 3 there could be a selection of the tax and the rate at which it was to be levied. In r. 4 what the Panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions made under cl. (c) and in the context and setting, the heading of r.5 brings out the scope of the rule. Therefore, the fixing of octroi limits with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy of tax duty. The figure of tax or levy of a tax or any further appeals to the Panchayat Simiti under section 124(5) does not alter the position in regard to time and place of publication.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1), of the , on a complaint by the Conciliation Officer against 5 accused persons, and the terms of reference were: " The conciliation proceedings were held, when a memorandum of the settlement is signed by the par ties to the dispute; (a) where no settlement is arrived at, when the report of the conciliation officer is received by the appropriate Government or when the work report is received under section 17, as the case may be; or (b) when a reference is made to a court Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under section 10 during the pendency of conciliation proceedings ". The appellants contended that on this interpretation the conciliation proceedings could not be said to be pending when the reference was received by an appropriate Government. Held, that the conciliation proceeding were in the present case after a period of more than 14 days and that is so there was no reason why the appellants should have been convicted under section 16(1). There was no illegality in the exercise of that right since the dispute in the instant case had not ended even before the expiry of 14 days, it would be to be to continue the criminal proceedings pending when a complaint is filed and not finally disposed of by the Government. Workers of the Industry Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the industry Colliery, ( ; , referred to. The settlement proceedings were therefore illegal. The provisions of section 12(6) of the Act did not support this contention as the termination of conciliation Proceedings was deemed to take place when the conciliation was received and when that report is delivered by theappropriate Government.

A large part of the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court was challenged by the Union of India, which was struck down by this court in Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona II Division while declaring unamended sec. 27 (6) of the Gold Control Act, 1968 as it stood prior to its amendment by the Amending Act No. 26 of 1969 constitutionally invalid on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down sec. 28 of the Act on the grounds that it has suffered from the infirmity of excessive delegate of legislative powers inasmuch as it imposed unreasonable delegation of limits and arbitrary power upon Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer, that the provisions confers an unguided, uncanive and uncanalised discretion upon the administrator with the resulting result that gross delegation of power by the Administrator when he chooses to negative the request cannot be struck down on the basis of excessive delegated legislation inasmuch as since no criteria nor guide lines had been provided for by reference and that such indefinite, uncertain and vague expressions or concepts had been used in some of the clauses under sec. 26(6) this Court struck it down secs. 28 and 29 of the Indian , as it stands prior to the amendment by section 26 of1969 and constitutionally invalid, on the view that the objective, the policy and the scheme of the Central Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the act afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec, 28 of Gold Control. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The objective object in putting the Act is to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. [955E,C] Harak Chand Banthria vs Union of lndia, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union Of India & Others, , followed. Harak Hiralal Banthia 's case while declaring amended sec.27(6), ultra vires the provisions of section 28 of tho Act valid. [964A C] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthia 's Case ; referred to.

The appellants claimed a declaration about their title to the properties in suit and for a permanent injunction restraining respondents 1 to 3 from interfering with their possession of the same. respondents Nos. 1 to3, who were appointed as trustees of the said temple obtained receipts from them that the properties belonged to the temple and that they were entitled to them. The appellants, who claimed to be the trustees of an alleged temple, resisted the suit on the ground that the lands had not been granted in Inam to the original grantee burdened with the obligation of performing certain services in a Matam. In the plaint (Ext. A 3) the properties had been resumed by the Collector and as such no question as regards the alienation was raised. The trial Judge also held that the appellants having proved their title on the lands, they were not entitled to possession. On appeal, the lower appellate court reversed the finding of the lower Appellate Court on the question whether the properties were 'conveyed in trust ' or manager '. On further appeal by special leave : HELD : The High Court erred in reversing the findings of the courts below though on a somewhat different ground. No other decision has been cited before the High Court which had accepted the proposition that article 134 B applied to suits instituted to set aside unauthorised alienation of endowed property by a Shebait or a Mahant or a manager of a Hindu religious endowment, was very uncertain prior to the suit was filed. [133 C D] The fact that the alienors had been removed from management of the temple had not be been considered by the High court. [134 E] District Court not having examined this aspect of the matter, and also, the findings recorded by the lower courts were right in decreeing the appellants ' suit in its entirety. [135 F G] The buildings that are attached to a Matan can be said to have changed one with another, but the fact remains that for more than 25 years or so, the management has been taken over by other persons who are acting as de facto managers of the Temple. Therefore, the question as to whether the lands were 'prowned in a temple falls outside the purview of article 134B can be raised. [136 G] In order that it may not be necessary for the defendant to show that the transfer was made on the basis that the property belonged to him or not to the religious endowment but to the manager himself ? [137 B C] The character of the representations made by the previous manager in regard to his relation with the property which is the subject matter of transfer, is irrelevant for the purpose of article134 A.

On July 22, 1966, the appellant decided to embark upon a venture to construct and operate an air conditioned Cinema in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. On June 17, 1969, Ved Gupta purporting to act on behalf of a partnership consisting of himself and the two persons aforementioned (as a matter of fact) applied to the District Magistrate, Jammu under section 3 of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 for permission to construct a modern cinema theatre in a portion of land in Gandhi hospital. The appellant objected that the cinema licence was revoked by the District Collector and in that connection, the State Government issued an order dated April 21, 1979 appointing an authorised person as the sole licensee. Pursuant to this order, the licensing authority, on December 3, 1977, suspended the licence for running the cinema theatre on the ground that the performance of his duties, namely, that he had knocked down at least two years prior to the date of the said order and thereby ceased to have any interest in the business of exhibition of cinematograph films. The District Magistrate rejected his request and transferred the license to another person. Thereafter, an application under section 6 F was filed by the appellant claiming that their names should also be included in the licence issued for Apsara Theatre from whom they had obtained from the Government for construction of the Theatre in question, had become final and that since the said procedure has not been followed by the licensing authorities, the impugned order was void and in violation of principles of natural justice. The High Court rejected this contention and set aside the order passed by the district Magistrate. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf on behalf appellant (i) that even though the licence had originally been issued in the name of Ved Gupta, the right of operation of the licence could not be made in the names of any party other than the original licensee, so long as there had not been any transfer of the license by the original license in favour of another with the permission of the licensing Authority. (ii) that under section 16(2) the powers to suspend a license pending the proceed ings for such revocation, the District magistrate had no power or a power to suspend the licence of the Cinema under any other circumstances; and (iii) that there was no occasion for the High Court, in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction envisaged by article 227, to issue a writ quashing the impugned orders. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Under section 16 (2) of the , in addition to the power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute, a licensee may also give an opportunity to the licensee to show cause why he should not be suspended by giving him a reasonable opportunity or as needed by any other person for having a reasonable cause. [580 F G] 1.2 In the instant case, on a reading of the provisions contained in the Act and the Rules and the explicit terms of the agreement itself it is impossible to sustain the view expressed in the judgment under appeal that the licence was granted for premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the appellant 's individual capacity and he alone was the licensee. [585 C] 1:3 The right title and claims of Shri Ved Gupta on the one hand and the firm and its partners on the other in respect of the Apsar Theatre are left open to be decided in the civil suit that is said to be pending.

The respondent was put in possession of a composite character consisting of three distinct matters. There were, firstly, a demise under which the mills and the factory in question were leased to them for a period of five years in accordance with the terms and conditions set out therein. Secondly, there was an agreement to sell the mills to the appellants in certain events and subject to certain conditions. The appellant claimed that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12 of the , which was rejected by the Custodian of Evacuee Property under sections 10 and 11 (1) of the . Held:(i) Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, (1953) S.C.R. 889, and Aswini Kr. Ghosh vs 80 Arabinda Mukherjee, [1950] 2 section C. R. 88, applied to leases granted by an evacuee and not by the evacuee. The operative portion of the section which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute; and that power cannot be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force" Though it was retrospective in operation, it did not affect the rights of the parties in the present case. Aswinikumar Ghosh vs Wohanbai A. Irani, ; , 21, 24 and Queen Empress vs Arabindinda Bose. (1953] S. C.R., 89, referred to. (ii) The respondent was acting within his authority in issuing Exhibit C in so far as it concerned the lease granted in favour of the appellants. Under section 12 the Act the Custodian had the power and had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. It could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law; but, not also by itself. But he did not do that thing. (iii) By section 12 it was the power of the Custodian in issuing the notice. As the notice was invalid under section 10 it applied only to the properties of the evacuee and it was not put forward for cancellation on their own contracts. Held, further, that the notice contained only two distinct matters and not one, namely, (i) whether the Custodian has the power under section 11 to cancel the lease in favour or (ii). The respondent had power and always the right to cancel such leases by his own contracts Held, also, that this provision was intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 did not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and could not have prevailed as against them; it could be done only if there was subsequent to the decision of the court below. (iv) The notice in terms refers firstly to the lease which it is proposed to cancel and thirdly to the movables in respect of which certain directions were given, and in their petition under article 226 it was contended that the respondent had no authority or power to issue a notice under section 13 of the Act to cancel an agreement of sale. Held also, further (per Kapur, J.).

The appellants were the erstwhile minor son of Raghubir Singh and his second writ petition was filed by his minor son Surendrapal Singh through his next friend Shri Jagjit Singh, maternal grand father of the minor. The relief claimed in both the petitions before the High Court was the same namely for setting aside of the order dated 6th August, 1977 passed by the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan, Ajmer and remanded the case to Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. Before the Division Bench of the High court in Second Writ Petition No. 681 of 1979 (Raghubir Singh vs The Board of revenue) it was urged that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. It was further contended on behalf of Raghubir singh, that the order of the Sub Divisional officer was erroneous as no appeal having been filed from the order the Sub division Officer dated 5th May, 1976, the said order became final and the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the sub division Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. In support of this contention it was submitted on behalf Of Raghubir Singh: that the State having not filed an appeal under Section 225 of the Act of 1955, and or revision under section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, the Board o/or the Revenue could not, while hearing the revision petition, set aside the orders of Sub Divisional Offi cer. Aggrieved by the order passed by Board of Ceiling for Rajasthan in Second Appeal No. 684 of 1979, the appellants filed a writ petition before the different High Court which was dismissed. It is contended on his behalf that section confers executive powers of superintendence and Control over subordinate revenue courts and it does not vest any power of superintendence on the Board on judicial side; that Section 9 is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Board over subordinate Revenue Courts and it is not applicable to judicial proceedings; and that the Board having appellate jurisdiction, could not make use of its powers of supervision and control and the order was not proper with reference to Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act. Dismissing the appeal by Special Leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court had recorded that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the impugned Act. It would be for the sub Divisional Officer to decide it in the light of the observations of the board. [728G] 1.2 Section 221 of the , is not subject to the other provisions of thesof the Act. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to the Board to interfere and set the matter right. The power is there, and it may be exercised sparingly in extraordinary case where interest of justice requires that the board should exercise the power. [ 728H] 1:3 Under Section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts 'and the applicant Raghubir Singh, his son Surendra Pal Singh, constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub divisional Officer, Bikaner for de novo determination of ceiling area for the appellant in law.

The respondent State of Maharashtra, the Central Government and its employees, who were working journalists in various newspapers, filed a writ petition in High Court challenging the validity of the order made by the Central Govt. on the recommendations of Justice Palekar Tribunal. Aggrieved by the decision of the Division Bench, the appellants filed this appeal by special leave. The first respondent contended that since the law authorities publishes in addition to the law the three years ' period ', the demand was unsustainable by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The expression `public news ' is of sufficiently wide amplitude to cover the publications of both the State and the employees employed by the Secretary of the Government as well as the employees incorporated in their respective newspapers. The appellant licensee was the monthly tenant of the suit premises and had let out to the respondent on or about the stipulated period. On or about 9th February, 1965 a fresh document of that date was executed and it was alleged that the licensor gave and granted his licence to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. The agreement recited that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. Clause 2 of the agreement recites that the licensees had given and granted the licensor a 'leave and Licence ' (which was the "licensor" and that it was agreed by the licensee that if he commits any default of any terms and conditions or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy the licensor shall be entitled to terminate the agreement and cancel and revoke and withdraw the leave and licence granted earlier and would be entitled lo take possession forthwith of the said workshop. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to him for conducting business and that he did so only in his possession as a licensee. The appellant further contended that he was a sub tenant, by the amendment to the effect from 1st September, 1965, as there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March 1966 the leaveand licence agreement between the parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order of eviction, this Court, HELD: (1) The expression 'licence ' is introduced and clause (2) said that it is only for the business purposes. [1059G] D.H. That in order to get the advantage of section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the premises, as a sub licensee as defined in section 5(4A) on the 1st of February 1973; but if permission to use land without exclusive possession was alone granted, a licence was the legal result. [ 1061G] (2)(a) The explanation to section 41 of the clearly indicates that it refers only to " license" and not the lease as defined by section 52 of the Easements Act, but also to "licence". [1060B C] (b) The language used and the restrictions put upon the use of the Premises in question by the appellant, indicate that the intention of the parties is the real test for ascertaining the character of a document. [ town planning Authority & Anr. vs Smt. Kaushalya Devi, ; and D.A. Devaraja Mudaliar vs T.V. Sarathnammal Chettiar, ; , referred to. (c) The understanding of the words "licence" would be that if permission is 'leyses in possession of the property, it is a lease; but, if it only permitted another to make use of this property, of which the legal possession continued with the owner, it was a licence; and so construed the intention would not amount to conferring the status and protection of a tenant. [1000D E] (d) The interpretation of the document in question is a license and not a lease.

Under the covenant in the State of Rajasthan, there was a merger and formation of a new State whereunder the former State of Dholpur came to be included in the United State ofRajasthan through the Matsya Union. The United State became the Part B State of Raj on January 26, 1950, when the Constitution came into force. Under article 295(2) of the Constitution, the State was bound by any obligation which might have arisen against the new State prior to the merger of Dholipur. However, a covenant in a contract entered into with the Ruler of the former Jodhpur State, provided for the continuance of all laws till they were repealed or amended by the new Provincial Legislature. The Rulers of Rajasthan and the States formed part B State on January 1, 1950. Thereafter, the United States of Rajasthan merged in India through the Calicut Union which merged in April 7, 1949. This covenant was subject to any agreement entered into between the Rulers of the erstwhile States including those who had formed the United state of Rajasthan. The Indian Independence Act 1947 was passed by the Ruler on January 17, 1950 and became law relating to the rights of citizens guaranteed by the Constitution. During the period when mergers were taking place after August 15, 1947 and ending December 2, 1947, the then United State was formed with the United Indian States. Under section 3 of these laws there was no right in the new sovereign to retain any of the powers of the Government of India under the Agreement entered into by the Rulers, nor was it bound by anything inconsistent with the Constitution or any other law made by him prior to January 26. 1950, by which all the old laws were repealed and altered or altered and so as to affect the rights and liabilities of the new States it was essential for the United Government of Rajasthan to undertake that liability. The respondent of the State sought refund of this amount paid under a notification issued by the Government on June 28, 1947. The suit was resisted by the State on several grounds but the High Court held that in view of article 295 (2) the State did not mean the United Chief Commissioner or the Ruler and that it could not be claimed to have been taken away by any law competently passed. On appeal to this Court it was contended inter alia, (1) that under article 295 of the Indian Constitution the Union had no right to forfeit the amount; (2), that even assuming that there was any right of the Ruler to forfeit such part of the sum paid by him in advance for not export he could only export 4,572 maunds and 20 seers after December 2. 1947; (3) that this section was repugnant to article 19(1)(f) and cl. (2); and (4) that even if there was some amount as refund on the merging State, such an amount did not exceed the contractual value. HELD: The provisions contained in the covenant under which the new and the liabilities arising there under or even otherwise, provided the law so made was within the competence of the Union Legislature and could not operate to confer any right on the company as against the old State. [183 B C] (1)(a) On the question whether the expression "Government" used in article 295 would include not only the United 'State of Rajasthan as it stood before January 26 but also the old States which came to different territories and those who formed the new nation after April 7. 1949, continued till they became repealed or altered into force were altered or modified by the existing Provincial Legislature after the Constitution coming into force it did not transgress the constitutional limitations.

The appellants were carrying on trade and business with high standards. It was urged that the provisions of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act (Mad XX of 1933) and the Rules framed thereunder, constituted an unreasonable restriction upon their fundamental right to do business and it was also contended that they did not only achieve the object for which they were enacted but defeat their purpose. Held, that the provision of the Act constituting reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's rights to do trade ,of business , is not merely unreasonable but is intended to benefit the large public. The imposition proposed by the Act is reasonable and must be supported by some material on record. The power conferred under section 18 of the said Act has to be exercised judicially, does not necessarily imply that there must be a clear and special definition. A person is exempt from the operation of the section in respect of any notified commercial crop. Every deduction in any transaction in respect Of the said agricultural crop other than those specified in the explanation is trade allowance for the purpose of the statute. The deductions cannot be received in any notified area by any person in any transactions in respect where such commercial crops are sold and the price paid for the sale. Therefore, the word 'trade allowance ' used in section 14 means trade allowance or not, must mean that all payments made to a specified person would be in any manner whatsoever connected with it. The purpose of section 14 is to protect the growers, the consumer and the seller. A trader who was having a licence to trade, in and about the place where the market is fixed, is deprived of his livelihood which is an unreasonable restrictions upon his right to deal trade in commercial crops because (a) the State Government issues a notification declaring their intention to exercise control over them; (b) the respondent had done so as to eliminate the middlemen and to give reasonable facilities for the growers of commercial crops to secure best prices for their commodities, and (c) the ban imposed by section 5 are not only unreasonable but tend to defeat its very purpose. The object of the provisions is to prevent the producers from having resort to distant markets with the result that they would be forced to give up their business and others would have to incur unnecessary expenditure which they could not afford. The Act is an integrated one and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial goods; trade involves the seller, the buyer, the commodity sold and price paid at the sale; under the section the said deduction should be in no transaction in regard to commercial crops.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death on the opinion that they were not guilty and so should be acquitted. Held, that though there was no evidence of any prior meeting between minds to form a pre arranged plan, there was nothing to indicate that they ran away together as a body or that they met afterwards. There was no reason why they should have been charged in the absence of further particulars. The fact that the accused were stated to have been wrongfully blamed by them did not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. Amika Bai vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. Veeraswami vs Emperor, and Mahbub Shah vs King Emperor, A.I.R. 1946 P.C 45, distinguished. jai Ammal vs King, (1924) L.R 52 I.A. 46 and Mahcbub Sahas case, not applicable. It was a question of fact in every case and there could be no scope for the proposition that section 377 Of the Code did not abrogate or modify the provisions which empowered the court to impose on it any material part of the body of the charges or were connected with the guilt of the accused. In order to establish one of the ingredients of common object or intention, the prosecution must prove affirmatively each ingredient and in all cases the accused charged should be tried together and convicted. A blow on the head with an axe which penetrates half an inch into the head is, in our opinion, likely to endanger life. The question of sentence in the case of Hodge vs Parker, , distinguished.

The petitioner who was a promotee in Class I service filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the order of compulsory retirement on the ground that he had attained the age of 50 years. [639F] 1:3 Sub clause(ii) carves Out a class Of Government servants into category and make a special Provision. According to sub clause A, sub cl.(ii) did not apply to the facts o f this case, as the peti tioner had not completed the age at all by the date of the order. One late Raja Vasireddi Chandra Dhara Prasad (hereinafter referred to as a 'deceased ') died intestate on 12th January, 1961. He had filled a proposal for insurance amount of Rs. 50,000 on 27th December, 1960. It was alleged in the plaint that there was medical examination by the doctor on the life of the deceased on 27st December,1960. The deceased had issued two cheques for Rs. 300 and Rs. 220 respectively in favour of the appellant as first premium. cheque for Rs 300 was encashed by the appellant on 29th December 1960. cheque was dishonoured three times and finally encashed on 11th January 1961. On 16th January. 1961, the widow of thedeceased respondent No. 1 wrote to the appellant intimating the death of the said deceased and demanded payment of Rs 50, 000. The Divisional Manager, Masulipatam Branch, denied liability on behalf of the Corporation, on 28th January as alleged in plaint was not true nor the alleged assurance if any, valid under law. On the 10th January 1964, the appellants filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulkotam which was dismissed by the Trial Court. The High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court dismissing the suit of the plaintiffs respondents against the appellant Corporation, holding that there had been no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation; and that the proposal, as per the prospectus of Life Insurance Corporation of India, the risk under the Corporation policy commenced on 11nd January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. It also held that the other averments in the claim, that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the corporation that the payment of the first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal and advised the deceased to pay the first premiums in full; were false. Allowing the appeal by certificate granted on 18th September, 1970 this Court HELD: 1. In view of the fact that such long time has elapsed and further in view of section 4 of the Act and the fact also that principal amount together with interest amounting to about Rs. 85,000/ have already been paid to the wife of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance, it would be adjusted towards premium amount; he stated that this purpose was to enable the Divisional Manager to asses the risk and take a decision according to the deponent. [360E F] 1:2. The expression "underwrite" signifies accepted liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. (See in the instant case, the Concise oxford Dictionary Sixth Edition p. 1267) It is true that normally the expression "Bywins and revivals" of policies in case of Life insurance Corporation and stated that it was the Divisional manager who was competent to underwrite policy for Rs 50.000 and above. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death or the preparation of a policy document, is not an acceptance. The first defendant had applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India Ltd. from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V/O Tractors Export, Moscow, on the ground that under a letter dated April 12, 1968, he granted an interim relief to the second defendant restraining encashment of letters of credit pending disposal of the suit. While the appeal was pending before this Court, the Bank filed applications for grant of the certificate under articles 133(1)(a) and 124 of the Constitution, and this Court held (Bachawat & Mitter JJ., dissenting) that an order granting interim injunction "is a final order" as far as it involved determining the rights of the parties within the meaning of article133 (1) of the Con stitution. Thereafter, in pursuance to the orders passed in those applications for revocation of the certificates granted by the High Court under articles 134(1), 133(2)(c) and 135(1) (b), such an order was not a final one within the terms of section 109 (a) as it was stated that the judgment, decree or final order was final if it finally disposed of the rights in the suit or proceeding. Where after the orders were made, the bank filed applications seeking amendment of the plaint to get effective relief. In appeal to this Court by special leave in respect of an interim order the High court held (i) that the expression "final order" occurring in article 133( 1 ) in the context in which it occurs meant a final adjudication by the Court of the right of the party, and that an interlocutory judgment even if it decided an issue or issues without finally determining the right and liabilities of the respective parties was not 'a judgment, however cardinal the issue may be. It must be held that on an examination of the merits of the case, this Court found (1 ) that an interim stay order passed by the Bombay High Court may become inoperative as framed and the plaintiffs may have to seek amendment of it to get appropriate relief, an order which is essentially an interlocutory order might be deemed final for the purposes of article 133 (1)(c), and (ii) that there was no distinction between a final decision on the rights and obligations of the par ties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suits. [704 B G] On the facts, this court held that an injunction order passed in certain cases may be deemed 'final for the purpose of article 134 (1).

In this writ petition, the petitioners assessee challenged the order of the Court on various grounds and the subject matter involved was considered in the case of the petitioner assessee assessee. Allowing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another, the information is required relating to the price at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agree to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. [346E] Rule 174 enjoins that the sale price at what he is selling of the goods must be the value of the grey cloth or fabric plus the value. of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is not necessary to include the operator 's profits who get the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [344F G] The price at Which he is sold must be taken as the value to which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise Authorities as the assessable value of such processed fabric and excise duty would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the prices at which he was selling the goods in a market, would include only the price or deemed price at that which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. [345A F] (a) Rule 174 does not require that when any goods owned on by one individual are manufactured, the duty is charged to him as the turnover of the processed fabrics or fabric and tax would be chargeable to the assessee on that account." [346C D] (b) The contention that the cost of packing allowing the price of permitting the packing of the packing material is a levyable burden has no substance.

Section 33 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961 provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1, 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the Amending Act shall continue to service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayat Samiti. The appellant was appointed as a Clerk in 1963 long before the Amending Acts came into force. Section 14(4) of the amending Act deleted section 33 of an Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The Amendment Act received the assent of the Governor on April 25, 1973. The State Government notified the absorption of the appellant as a clerk though, as stated earlier he was working as a Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti and was appointed substantively to that post in the Department of time. On January 21, 1974 he was appointed temporarily as a clerks on an ad hoc basis in January 1974. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samiti sent back the appellant 's appointment as a head clerk on an officiating basis. Later he was promoted as a SubHead Clerk on an Ad hoc basis on April 1 1975 and which became a senior scale with effect from June 13, 1973 when the Amending act came into operation. The amendment Act received assent on April 15, 1973, and was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 13. 1973. Section 17 of the Act deleted the section 33 by the Amending Amendment Act of 1973. By this amending Act the Panchayat Sabha Samiti lost its power to appoint a Head clerk as a result of the deletion of section 33. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court praying that he should be absorbed as a new Head Clerk and the respondent be absorbed in Government service, as a Junior Accountant prior to his absorption in Government Service. Both parties adduced evidence. A single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled for promotion from the date on which it purported to do so. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD:1. The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, What is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be treated for promotion but, whether the Panchayat has the right to appoint him to the post as of Head clerk on the date of his appointment on which he purported to doing so. Clearly it had fortified that right on June 23, 1973 because he was employed lawfully to the Post of a Sub Registrar. He was appointed lawfully to tho post of a Head Office and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him.

The question for decision was whether the fund, which were purchased by Mahant Shivshankar Yati and who owned a certain private properties in village Amauli, could be regarded as his personal property. The plaintiff filed a suit claiming that the property belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math. He asserted that the Dharamshas were purchased from the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivpher Yati. In the course of assessment proceedings under U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948 the Amauli properties were described by Mahant Ram Shivs ShankerYati, and not that of the Math or the temple. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969 holding inter alia that the Amaiuli properties had been purchased by Math Sri Shivs Shankar Yati in 1921 from his personal and independent funds inherited in his favour from his predecessors Shivphar Yati, which included the properties in the village Amai uli. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclean and must therefore be regarded for exemption from the levy was made. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The income from the properties belonging to the Mahant Shiv Shankar Yatati and Mahant Shiv shankar Yatti are not a part of the properties of Math or of deity, Sri Thakur, Gokarnendraeshwar Mahadeoji. [663 F] 2. Where a nuakerus of endowed property exists the acquisition Of additional property must be attributed lo the application clause of the deed. [665 G] 3. There is no presumption either way. All the facts and circumstances must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to the math or deity or is the personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. [664 D] [The Commissioner for Hindu Religious Endowments vs M/s. Oriental Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts, ; referred to.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan had been granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. Rule 2 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Rules (Andhra Area) Rules (which was amended by 1976), provided that every Government employee, not being a workman and not belonging to the last grade Service shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attained the age of 60 years. Clause 10(2) provides that every government employee, other than in the last Grade Service, who had already attained the minimum age of 55 years was to retire from serv ice on the evening of the first day of a month in his service from the afternoon on the expiry of which he attains the age Of 55 years. The petitioners were retired from service prematurely by a notification dated October 29, 1979 and no opportunity had been given by it to its employees before reducing the age, of retirement from 58 to 58. The Government issued an order stating that it had decided to reduce the age in question of superannuation for all Government employees, other except in cases of technical personnel and moral staff, and that it was revealed that on account of the increase in the age retirement from 55 to 60 years in 1976, a vested right had accrued to the employees, which could be taken away if at all only from future entrants to the Government service; that the age Small, Small and Industrial Engineering Service, which had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths h Is no relevance on the question of fixing the age. The writ petitions filed by the petitioners were allowed by a learned single Judge as well as by a Division Bench of the High Court and the decision of the Government was upheld by this Court in State of Mysore vs P. D. Sharma, [1974] 2 S.C.R. 971. In these appeals it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amendment to the Fundamental Rules was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature and that the court was wrong in holding that the impugned order was bad because (a) the recommendation made by the Pay Commission was casual and not based on relevant criteria; (b) the Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the age and (c) the question whether the amendment violates Articles 14 and 16. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The petition must succeed. It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended as they can be made, under the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 and that, the power to amend these rules carries with it the power of amendment, by which the proviso thereto was deleted retrospectively, was a valid exercise of legislative power.

The appellants are a registered dealer in the State of Haryana. He purchased raw materials in the state without paying tax thereon, in view of the provisions of section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. On these facts, it was claimed that the assessee is not liable to pay purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. This claim has been rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court and hence these appeals. The main question for determination in all these appeals is whether the sales effected by the assessees fall within one of the exempted categories set out in sec tion 9(i)(b) which exempts only sale made in the course of export outside the territory of India. HELD: 10. In cases covered under section 5(1)(a)(ii), there can be no dispute that a tax is leviable under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on their sales as well as purchases. [353C] C.W.P. 1227/80, dated 1st April, 1976, which was also affirmed by a Division Bench later 2; and C.A. No. 128 of 1981 dated 2nd April, 1983, which is also affirmed in appeal by a single Judge of the High COurt having decided the issue against the assessees as early as 25.11.1980 in C. A. Nos. 128 (f) and 353 (b).

The goods of the assessees were sent to an address outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by M/s. Daulatram Rameshwarlal, in respect of the castor oil sold to some persons and that they became owners of the goods after shipment. The sellers filed their return of turnover for the years 1954 1960 59 and 1955 56 under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on the ground that these sales were oil FOB contracts under which they continued to be the owners of those goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and so no tax was realisable on them. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption and assessed them to sales tax on a taxable turnover including these sales. On appeal by the sellers, the High Court held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till they had been brought on board ship and therefore it held that there was no circumstance which would justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales were on FOB contracts Property in the goods would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. Held, that if at the time of export the proper commences. after the goods cross the customs frontier is crossed the import has taken place out of the territory of India. It was not correct to say that though a person has not made a false declaration of his intention, the fact remains that the intention declared has not been carried out.

The respondent husband married the appellant (wife) as a second wife, way back in 1956, and a few years later had a son by her. The initial warmth vanished that both of them had been divorced from July 1962, and that she had received, whether before or after the date of the said order, the whole of the sum which under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties, was payable on such divorce cancela tion. For some time there was flickering improvement in the relations between the husband and the quondum wife and they lived together. Later they separated became entranged; the appellant finding herself in financial straits and unable to maintain herself moved the magistrate under section 125 Cr. P.C., 1973 for a monthly allowance of maintenance. The sessions judge who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her a child. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by way of a revision application in which it was contended that: (1) under section 127(3)(b) of the Cr.P.C. 1973, the Magistrate had no jurisdication to consider whether the applicant was a divorcee and as such was ineligible for maintenance; (2) under sub section (4) of section 125 by virtue of the compromise decree, the appellant 's client was still entitled to an allowance; and (3) there must be proof of neglect to maintain attract section 125(4) in the absence of proof that the lady was not living separately by mutual consent. The Sessions Judge dismissed a revision petition filed by the aggrieved husband. On appeal the High Court, while affirming the order of the Sessions judge, observed that it is for the wife and not for her parents or others, to prove mutual consent to live apart from divorce painfully implies that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. Allowing the appeal of the appellant, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of sections 127(4)(b), 125 and sister clauses must receive a compassionate expansion of sense that the words used permit. The Special Leave Petition is allowed. [79F] 2.2 The appeal should be dismissed.

The appellant who was a defaulter in the shop of the respondent State Government alleged that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In so far as the first part of the order directing that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect of future contracts, cannot he sustained in law. The earlier order was set aside by this Court in a Writ Petition filed under Article 32 of the Constitution by the State Government. On behalf of the State it was contended that there is no requirement specifically of giving such prior notice as there has been no requirement expressly of giving the prior notice after black listing and an opportunity of making representation. Before this Court it was submitted on behalf of Respondent State that there had been no response to the earlier order since the only ground for cancellation of the bid has been stated in the earlier Writ Petition that there has not been any requirement specifically as required by clause 5(a) of the Rule giving any notice and therefore, the cancellation of candidature of the appellant was setaside. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the premises, that portion of the impugned order directing the appellant to be placed with the black List in respect thereof cannot be sustained in Law. [867H; 869A] 2.1 Rule 5(b) of Central Excise Rules provides that no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal black listing the appellant. It is an implied principle of the rule and of law that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. The rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. [861A] 3.2 In the instant case, no notice has been given for giving any reason and there was therefore no requirement which specifically requires of giving a prior notice.

The High Court of Mysore held that the case now before this Court was also governed by what was held in Shankariah 's case. The petitioner contended (i) that he was not heard after the final list was prepared, because, some mistakes had crept in due to want of heating on two points; (ii) that the objection raised by the petitioner in his petition was covered by Shankari h 's writ application which had been dismissed by the Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The respondents were entitled to an opportu nity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by the peti tioners before it. Accordingly, the combined final gradation List dated April 6, 1962 was published, so far as category 6 was concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [207 G] 5. The combined final final gradation lists dated April 3, 1962 so faras category 6 is concerned, are therefore ultra vires.

The appellant company manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Act. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil is a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture, it was stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of appellant that the word "cost" in sub section (4)(d)(i) of Section 4(4)(D)(i), as amended by Act 9 of 1984, included the cost of packing in the value of goods when the packing was supplied by a customer to a manufacturer on its own cost. The respondent Collector, while determining the assessable value, made an order for assessment under Section 35L(b) of the Act, which was accepted by him and accordingly, he levied duty thereon. On revision, the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal held that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and containers were not returnable by the buyer there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable valuation. It also held that since at the date of removal, the goods fell within the definition of "packing" in Section 4 (4) (d)(ii)(i). In the appeals under Section 36L(B) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944, it could not be said that even though in that case that fact 10% of its production were only retail sales would not affect the question of determination of the assessablevalue of the excisable goods with reference to its value in the wholesale market. The Revenue contended before this Court that the cost involved was not includible in the valuation of the goods since these were only ancillary and not incidental to the activities for the manufacture of gases, but the value could not he included in that assessable value. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of Section 3 of the Central Excises and Salt Act 1944, the cost and potentiality of packing is taxable at the depot gate. [994C D] 1.2 The cost of the containers to the buyer has to be added to the price except where the packing is of durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. If on the other hand, the manufacturer asks the customer to bring his own container and does not charge anything therefore then the cost (or value) of such packing cannot be "notionally" added to, or subtracted from, the price at which the goods have been sold by the manufacturer .

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the appellant, demanding bribe of Rs. 100. The prosecution case was that the appellant sent for PW 1, informing him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of RS. 100, which was on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant that the food served in the canteen was substand ard. Since the appellant had failed to comply with the demand, the appellant was charged under section 161 I.P.C., and he pleaded that there was no extention for payment of bribe as there had been no occasion for doing so. The Trial Court accepted the defence evidence, rejected the plea of the appellant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that there had not been any independent evidence regarding the demand of bribe. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1(i) Where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be rebutted by 'proof ' and not by bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the Explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to have been rebutted. [338G H, 339A B] 2(ii) The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. The plea of innocence raised before this Court was also not impressive. [336E F] State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; C.I. Ernden vs State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1964 SC 575; and Lohana Kantilal vs State, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1 921 referred to.

The respondent company was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited, a Government of india undertaking after obtaining release from Government service. The petitioner retired from the service of the company on or about September 30, 1984. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave. However, the company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act 1971 and obtained ad interim stay of the proceedings before the Estate officer. The Estate Officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner.
