It was contended for the petitioner that the provision contained in Section 630 of the Act is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to strict construction and there is no room for intendment. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'from the context in which it appears is, must take its colour from the context, in which the language appears. [177A] 2.2 Where an officer or employee of a company wrongfully obtains possession of any property of the Company during the course of his employment, to which he is not entitled, the acts of delinquency ' specified in clauses (a) and (b) thereof. He may also take in past officers and employees. The words "any such property" in clause (b.) relate to any property mentioned in cl. (a). [177B C] Amritlal Chum vs Devi Ranjan Jha & Anr., ; , referred to. 2.3 The expression 'any such thing ' occurring in sub section (1) of Section 630 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employee but also to include past officers or employees, and also to past officers. There is therefore no warrant for the construction placed by the High court on the provisions contained in section 630(1). [178E F] 2:4 The words 'any other such property ' in cl.(b) are separated by the word 'or ' which must take their colour from context in Which it appears. The whole object of enacting sub section 1 of Section 642 is the preservation of the property of a Company by the creation of two distinct offences by clauses (b), (d) and that which arise under different sets of circumstances, and it would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl.

The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. After the passing of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons Bhaskarrao Chimanrao Deshmukh and Ramkrishna Tryambak Deshpande as constituted attorneys of Vasudeobuwa who was described in the application as the 'owner ' of the property. The name of the Trustee is Sakharam Maharaj. The application was made on May 29, 1952 to the Assistant Charity Commissioner under protest and without prejudice to the claim made therein that the Sansthan was not a public trust. In view of the penal provision under section 66 of the Act in the case of non compliance with section 18(1) of the Bombay Public Trust Act the said application was filed ex abundanti cautela. The Assistant Charity commissioner after requisite notice again made an enquiry into the matter and held that the temple to be a private property and not apublic trust. The District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner by his order of October 16, 1959. It is against this order the present appeal was filed on special leave granted by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: (1) In view Of the penal provisions under section 116 of the Trusts Act the application was ' made ex abunditi cautely. [518 A] (2) The expression in the recital that 'you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour favour of an individual as private property. [525 E F] According to the appellant this would go to show that the executant of the document as if he was appointed by the Maharaj who happens to be holding the Gadi at the relevant time. The fact that the life time of the recited temple has now been treated by those who are connected with the management as intended for user by the public without restriction, makes no difference in this case. [511 C] (3) The object and purpose for which the trust was created is the maintenance of that worship for the benefit of worshippers, the question whether an endowment is private or public presents no difficulty. The expression "in the recital" merely refers to Shri Vithal Harirao Deshmukh as Manager. ' It does not alter or convert the said gift which cannot be treated as a "private property". [525 G H] (4) In the present case all the above tests are fulfilled.

Where a citizen who was a resident in India was sought to be detained for more than six months by the Income tax Officer for having held certain private limited companies, the Income Tax officer issued a warrant of arrest against him under section 46(2) and (3) directing his arrest. The Sales Tax Officer attached the goodwill and tenancy rights in the said premises by a warrant and directed the Income Income Tax Officer to recover from such person the amount specified therein as if it were an arrear of land revenue: Held, that the Income ' tax Officer had no power under section 48 for recovery of arrears of land Revenue. The expression "any sum due" used in section 46 (2) as meaning "any sums due by a company to an assessee as well as "other person ". If in the matter of recovery of dues of land revenues defaulters of one State cannot complain of denial of equal protection of laws on the ground of the difference, in the modes of recovery prevailing in other States, can it be said to be unreasonable for the Union to adopt, for the recovery of its public demand from defaulters of each state, the same mode of recovery (1) ; , 157. 163 Erimmal Ebrahim Hajee vs The Collector of Malabar, ; , approved. That the assessment proceedings had been started and the certificate issued by the Sales Tax officer in respect of other limited companies was not invalid under article 13(1) of the Constitution as it was originally amended and the warrant of attachment was issued on the 7th June 1955.

Some workmen of the respondent Port Trust, were employed by the present appellant Trust Employees ' Union. The Trustees first introduced a two shift system called "Pahal Docks on June 30, 1953 and the same system was extended to the Prince 's and Victoria Docks. The workmen who were represented by the Port Trust General Workers ' Union made a demand for a fixed recess of one hour and thereafter they were informed that if the demand be pressed a three shift system would be introduced. The award also directed that in the event of failure to comply with all the provisions the rules regarding payment of overtime wages should be paid. The Union recognised certain hours of work on a system of lock gates which enabled the depth of water at the docks to be artificially regulated but the Prince "s and Hill Drew" went up to 9 hours 'clock and reached only a few minutes later. The Officers apprehended that this was a device to get 4 hours ' overtime and rejected the demand. An industrial dispute arose between the workmen and respondents. The matter in controversy was stated by the parties to be : (1) Whether the existing system of work required any modification; (2) whether the period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift, and some times at the end depending on the tides or the exigencies of the work. The Standing Orders provided for a revision of the rates of wages by raising the rate of duty at which no allowance could be claimed; (3) Whether there should be a fixed machine for rest but also for the work load in relation to wages, and (4) Whether overtime was the only one which could be made up on a day. HELD: The workmen were entitled, if present for work, for overtime up to four hours but they must pay a double rate for any hour or part of an hour of actual work in excess of 9 hours.

Under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the provisions of sections 39, 40, 41 & 45 were applicable to this case. Section 2(2)(a) of the Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1) a suit for eviction on the grounds mentioned in Cl. (a) to sub section(2) shall be pending on the date of commencement of the said Act. Section 39 deals with the jurisdiction of the civil court and also provides that where any building is constructed substantially out of funds obtained by way of loan or advance from the State Government or the Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a cooperative society or a Co operative Society or the Uttar Pradesh Chits Evam Vikas Parishad, and the period of repayment of such loan or advances exceeds the aforesaid period of ten years then the reference in this sub section to the period for which the first assessment thereof comes into force shall be deemed to be a reference to the time of fifteen years or the period ending with the date when the last assessment of this property was made. In view of the language of section 39 and 40 even if the matter is pending in this Court, the protection would be available to the appellant but looking to the language contained in that provision it appears that the contention of the respondent landlord that the rights of parties will be governed on the basis of the date on which the suit was filed and it was contended that if on the day on which that Act came into force, the construction is completed, the period from which 10 years are to be computed would be the date at which the First assessment of the property was first made. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The pro visions of section 40 must be read in a manner as to give the benefit thereof to the tenant if the conditions contemplated in those sections are satisfied. It is true that this Section applies not only to suits pending on tho date of the commencement of this Act and it cannot be contended that the present revision petition or the appeal either to the High Court or the appellate authority arose out of suit which was pending on that date, but this contention could not be accepted as it is very clear from the language in the Section itself. In the light of the discussion above the question whether during the pendency of the proceedings 10 years have elapsed the tenant is entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in the said section. [164F G] 1.2 The lease in question was, therefore, not hit by section 20(1)(a). [164G H] 1:3 In the instant case it is clear that during the proceedings in this court 10 years had elapsed even if this Court and 10 years of expire even if a date of completion is taken to be 1.10.76 which is the date for filing of the suit, one year has to be calculated from the date indicated in Explanation 1 and it is, therefore concluded by a decision of this court in Manchanda Amar Nath Basheshar Dass 's case [1985] 3 SCR 491 that if during the course of proceedings 10 year have elapsed, the tenant will be entitled to all the benefits of the provision of the U .P. Act, 1947.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of the three appellants from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1, Shibtola Lane, Entally, Calcutta). The appellant contested the suit on the ground that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties and had based his claim before the Munsif under section 3 of the Act as amended by an Amending Act of 1953 introducing important changes in the Act of 1949 so as to afford any protection to the respondent. The trial court dismissed the suit but the first appellate Court on a consideration of the provisions of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1952, held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 4 in view of the amendment made by the Act. On appeal to the High Court, HELD: The decision of the High court is right inasmuch as the landlord made no attempt to establish any of the grounds mentioned in s.3. [176 B] The fact that after the coming into force of the , it was not open to the landlord to file a suit, did not mean that he could claim the benefit under section 4 of the amended Act of 1951 by his application for relief provided delivery of possession had not been given to the decree holder. This is because before the Ordinance of 1952 no one could establish his rights as a thika tenant in view Of the vague definition of "thika tenant" in the Calcutta & Thika Zamindari Tenancy ( Amendment) Ordinance, 1952. [177 F G] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, I.L.R. , followed. Mahade Kolal Kanara Kanodia and Anr. vs Administrator, General of Madras, ; , referred to. In the instant case, unless there was anything to show that the tenant was entitled tO eject him after taking into account s.4 of section 3 he would not be entitled to eject his tenant. [174 E] Mahaddeol Mal Kanodia V. Administrator General for West Bengal and Anr., I. L.R , approved.

Prior to 1965 in the High Court Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were in the pay scale of Rs. 354 320 as against the pay scales of Rs, 120 300 to Section Officers and Rs. 500 1,000 respectively. In 1965, the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference to their pay scale. The Committee recommended a pay scale slightly lower than that laid down by the Pay Commission. The recommendation was rejected. Aggrieved, the appellants filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging its decision on the ground that: (1) the Bench Secretaries cannot be given the same scale of pay which is being given to Superintendents or Section Officers; and (2) the creation of two Grades with different pay scales cannot amount to discrimination. Dismissing the appeal and setting aside the judgment, this Court, HELD: 1. The Pay Commission refused to equate Bench Secretaries with Section Officers in view of their differential duties. It was found that the nature of duties and responsibilities of both posts could not be said to be equal. Keeping in view the fact that vacancies in Upper Division/Lower Division Assistants are filled up by promotion from Routine Grade Assistants, it is clear that this is a second promotion for those who come directly to Lower division Assistants and a third promotion for these persons who are promoted first to Upper Division Assistant and then a Bench Secretary. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. [298A] 2. It is true that at one time, Judges Secretaries were paid more emoluments than Section Officers but it was not known on what basis they were paid in the higher pay scales and treated as a superior class to Section officers. But it is not known when exactly Anomaly Committee redressed the wrong by granting pay scale equivalent to section Officers, it created an artificial division by drawing a line between first ten and others. On this view, all Bench Secretaries of Grade I have to bear more responsibilities in their Section and have to control over its subordinates.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries. On January 10, 1942, an agreement was entered into between the Rajah of Venkatagiri and one Sri Balumuri Nageswara Rao whereby the Raja agreed to give annual leases in respect of certain slate leases within his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942 if the Rajah was satisfied with the work carried on by the lessee during the preceding year. The lease was extended further to 21st July, 1945, but after 21st August, 1944, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease grant. Although there was no response by the respondent to this request, the application was rejected by his order dated December 27, 1955. In the meantime on September 21, 1955, the Government of India Act, 1935, came into force and on October 1, 1947, the suit lands were notified under section 3 of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, which was later extended to 22nd January, 1945. On April 23, 1956, the Collector issued an order declaring that the lease granted earlier to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945 and that as the lease was for a period exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20 (1) of the Abolition Act. The question before this Court was whether the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights by the order dated 12th December, 1955 was bad because it did not give three months ' notice, as required by section 20 of the Act. Held, that the notice dated January 13, 1952, fell under the second Proviso and is valid. The words " such rights" refer to rights created prior to 1st July 1945, would be valid; (ii) those rights created after July 1. were only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction.
